statement: Across New York City community districts, hotter daytime surface temperature goes with a higher rate of heat-stress emergency department visits, and this survives adjustment for poverty, percent Black residents and household air conditioning.

graph_evidence.summary: Sun et al. 2021 (BMJ, 74 million insured US adults, 2010-2019): days at the local 95th percentile of warm-season temperature had 66.3% (60.2 to 72.7) excess risk of ED visits for heat-related illness, with stronger effects in the Northeast. Stowell et al. 2023 (US children): OR 1.34 (1.16 to 1.56), ages 6-12.
Bernhard et al. 2015 (Alabama): income above $20K associated with lower personal heat exposure, beta -1.05 C (-1.79 to -0.30), through the home thermal environment.

graph_evidence.relationship_id: (concepts I2CN3brExA tree, lHLIKbfnYp green space, RF7tCwCaa5 vegetation cover)
graph_evidence.summary: The tree concept has no relationships. Green space has 14, none with temperature, heat illness or emergency care. Surface temperature links only to air temperature (r about 0.9, 2 studies), population density (r 0.82) and deforestation (r 0.89). No finding connects trees or green space to heat-related ED visits.

literature.citation: Madrigano J, Ito K, Johnson S, Kinney PL, Matte T. A case-only study of vulnerability to heat wave-related mortality in New York City (2000-2011). Environ Health Perspect 2015;123:672-678.
literature.finding: Heat-wave deaths in NYC were more likely among Black residents and in areas with less green space and higher surface temperature (case-only design).

literature.citation: NYC DOHMH Environment and Health Data Portal, Heat Vulnerability Index (NTA); and EHDP-data repository, key-topics/heat-vulnerability-index.
literature.finding: The HVI is built from surface temperature, green space, household air conditioning, poverty or median income and percent Black residents, chosen because they predicted heat-related deaths. Using the HVI as an outcome of trees would be circular.

literature.citation: Sun S et al. Ambient heat and risks of emergency department visits among adults in the United States. BMJ 2021;375:e065653.
literature.finding: 95th vs median warm-season temperature (34.4 C vs 14.9 C national average): heat-related illness ED visits +66.3% (60.2 to 72.7).

prediction.magnitude: Unadjusted: +3% to +15% in the age-adjusted heat ED rate per 1 F of surface temperature. Adjusted for poverty, percent Black and AC: attenuated by at least a third, +0% to +8% per 1 F, with an interval that may include zero.
prediction.support_if: adjusted slope positive with lower 95% limit above 0 (confirmed link)
prediction.refute_if: adjusted slope negative with upper limit below 0

plan: Unit: 59 community districts. Outcome: EHDP indicator 2443 (heat stress, 5-year ED visits, average annual age-adjusted rate per 100,000, measure 1405, CD), log scale; secondary outcome EHDP 2410 (10-year heat hospitalizations, age-adjusted, measure 1283). Exposure: EHDP 2141 surface temperature (F). Covariates from hvi-nta.csv averaged to CD: POV_PCT, PCT_BLACK_POP, PCT_HOUSEHOLDS_AC. Model: OLS of log rate on surface temperature, unadjusted and adjusted, HC3 SE; report percent change per 1 F. Secondary unit: NTA2010, HRI_HOSP_RATE from hvi-nta.csv on SURFACETEMP with the same covariates.
alternatives: Poverty and race drive both residence in hot, treeless districts and ED use (insurance, ED as usual source of care, outdoor work)
Residents are exposed where they work and travel, not only where they live
ED rates count residents by home address; small counts in some CDs are unstable
